Recent work supports combining local transitions with sequence models. GaGNN (2024) uses group-level and individual transition graphs to supplement sparse histories ([paper](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ins.2024.120623)). A 2026 benchmark audit finds that retrieving through a few-hop item-transition graph from the last one or two items, then ranking by feature similarity, competes with sophisticated models across several datasets, including Amazon CDs. Its explanation—low branching, feature-smooth transitions, weak dependence on long histories—suggests measuring these properties before adding complexity; its reported gains are not evidence for the pinned RecHarness setup ([preprint](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.07125)).

Text similarity alone does not establish directional complementarity. ST2SI (COLING 2025) explicitly identifies missing item-transition learning as a weakness of text-based recommendation, but uses an LLM and therefore is not directly eligible under the no-pretrained-weights constraint ([paper](https://aclanthology.org/2025.coling-main.171/)). A constraint-compatible research hypothesis is a SASRec residual combining a sparse directed transition score with title/description token embeddings trained from scratch on the allowed corpus. Separate source and destination projections can represent asymmetric next-item relationships; normalized transition counts and shrinkage can limit popularity effects and unreliable rare edges. Keep semantic similarity as a separate signal, with validation-selected fusion weights. These are proposed adaptations, not verified findings from a matching paper; observed chronological transitions indicate predictive association, not proven product complementarity.
